title: Let's (not) just put things in Context: Test-time Training for Long-context LLMs
claim: As input length grows, in-context accuracy and extra thinking tokens degrade or stall, while a small amount of test-time training keeps improving.
layout: 3 panels left-to-right, two line plots then bar chart, shared legend below
description: Three side-by-side plots share one legend underneath. Panels (a) and (b) are line plots with dots. The x-axis is context length: number of code lines in (a), number of transactions in (b). The y-axis is accuracy (%). Three colored lines run through each panel: tan for In-Context Only, orange-red for With Thinking, and teal for With Query-only Test-Time Training (qTTT). Accuracy falls as context grows. The tan line falls fastest, to near zero. The orange line falls more slowly and flattens. The teal line stays highest at long lengths. Panel (c) is a grouped bar chart of gain over in-context accuracy for Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-8B. Each model has an orange bar (+3, +10) and a taller teal bar (+11, +17), with the gains labeled above the bars. Captions (a), (b) and (c) sit under the panels. The eye goes first to the teal curves and bars.
caption: Query-only test-time training uses inference-time compute more effectively than “thinking” tokens for long contexts. (a, b) We construct two tasks to perform controlled long-context analysis: (a) bug localization in large code repositories, and (b) anomaly detection in transaction logs. As context length T grows, in-context accuracy drops and thinking tokens show diminishing returns; with the same FLOP budget, qTTT consistently improves performance. (c) qTTT shows improvements across domains and model sizes on LongBench-v2 and ZeroScrolls benchmarks.
abstract: Progress on training and architecture strategies has enabled LLMs with millions of tokens in context length. However, empirical evidence suggests that such long-context LLMs can consume far more text than they can reliably use. On the other hand, it has been shown that inference-time compute can be used to scale performance of LLMs, often by generating thinking tokens, on challenging tasks involving multi-step reasoning. Through controlled experiments on sandbox long-context tasks, we find that such inference-time strategies show rapidly diminishing returns and fail at long context. We attribute these failures to score dilution, a phenomenon inherent to static self-attention. Further, we show that current inference-time strategies cannot retrieve relevant long-context signals under certain conditions. We propose a simple method that, through targeted gradient updates on the given context, provably overcomes limitations of static self-attention. We find that this shift in how inference-time compute is spent leads to consistently large performance improvements across models and long-context benchmarks. Our method leads to large 12.6 and 14.1 percentage point improvements for Qwen3-4B on average across subsets of LongBench-v2 and ZeroScrolls benchmarks. The takeaway is practical: for long context, a small amount of context-specific training is a better use of inference compute than current inference-time scaling strategies like producing more thinking tokens.
